title: Pressure-cooker chicken curry
subtitle: A rich, saucy curry without the long simmer
excerpt: Chicken thighs in a spiced tomato and coconut sauce cooked under pressure. The sauce thickens around the meat in 15 minutes, a warming curry that is ready faster than a takeaway.
sourceNotes: British chicken curry is a broad category influenced by South Asian cooking traditions and adapted through generations of British Indian restaurants and home cooks. This version follows the general method of toasting whole spices, building an onion-tomato base, and adding meat to simmer, here compressed by the pressure cooker.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool completely and freeze in airtight containers for up to 4 months. Defrost overnight in the fridge and reheat in a saucepan, stirring, over medium heat.
recipe.batchNotes: This recipe doubles well. Freeze half in individual portions.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The curry is better the next day. Refrigerate for up to 3 days and reheat gently.

content.text: Pressure-cooker chicken curry gives you a saucy, deeply spiced result without the hour of gentle simmering that stovetop curries usually need. Chicken thighs hold up well under pressure, staying juicy and absorbing the sauce rather than drying out. The pressure-cooked sauce is rich and thick, the spices have nowhere to evaporate to.

The sauté phase before sealing the lid matters. Onion cooked until properly soft and golden, spices toasted briefly in the hot fat, and tomato puree stirred until it darkens slightly, these three steps cannot be skipped or accelerated. The pressure cooker does the rest, but it starts from this foundation.
Serve with basmati rice or naan. A spoonful of plain yoghurt and some fresh coriander at the table complete the dish.

Set the pressure cooker to sauté or use the open pot on the hob. Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring occasionally, for 10 minutes until golden. Add the garlic and ginger; cook for 1 minute. Add the ground cumin, coriander, turmeric, and chilli powder; stir for 1 minute. Add the tomato puree and stir for 1 more minute until it darkens.

Add the chicken pieces and stir to coat in the spice base. Add the tinned tomatoes and {{coconut-milk}} of coconut milk. Season with salt and stir through. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 12 minutes, then quick-release.
Open the lid and stir in the garam masala. Taste and adjust the seasoning. If the sauce is thinner than you like, set the open pot over medium heat and simmer for 5 minutes.

rows.symptom: The curry sauce is too thin
rows.cause: The onions released more moisture than expected, or the tinned tomatoes had more liquid than usual.
rows.fix: Simmer in the open pot over medium-high heat for 5 to 10 minutes, stirring, until the sauce reduces to a coating consistency.

rows.symptom: The spices taste raw or sharp
rows.cause: The spices did not toast long enough in the hot fat before liquid was added.
rows.fix: Always stir dry spices in the hot pot for a full minute before adding any liquid. This blooms the spices and removes the raw edge.

rows.cause: Breast meat was used instead of thighs, which dries under pressure.
rows.fix: For next time, use boneless thighs. If the current batch is dry, stir the meat through the sauce and allow it to absorb over a few minutes.

content.text: This curry is significantly better the following day when the spices have had time to settle. Refrigerate for up to 3 days or freeze in portions for up to 4 months. Reheat from frozen or from the fridge in a saucepan over medium heat, stirring occasionally.

Chicken curry is part of the everyday British cooking repertoire. It arrived through South Asian immigration and restaurant culture, was adapted by home cooks and cookbook writers from the 1970s onwards, and is now one of the country's most regularly cooked weeknight dishes. The pressure cooker version makes it faster without sacrificing the depth that distinguishes a good home curry from a rush job.
